claim: tgt is required for optimal growth of Vibrio cholerae in the presence of sub-lethal aminoglycoside concentrations.
source: tgt is required for optimal growth of Vibrio cholerae in the presence of sub-lethal aminoglycoside concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study, specifically competition experiments and growth assays showing growth defects of Δtgt in sub-MIC tobramycin.

claim: Tgt is the enzyme modifying the guanine (G) in tRNAs with GUN anticodon to queuosine (Q).
source: Tgt is the enzyme modifying the guanine (G) in tRNAs with GUN anticodon to queuosine (Q).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of Tgt enzyme.

claim: Q34 impacts the efficiency of decoding at tyrosine TAT and TAC codons.
source: Using molecular reporters, we showed that Q34 impacts the efficiency of decoding at tyrosine TAT and TAC codons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using GFP reporters with codon stretches and β-lactamase reporters.

claim: The anti-SoxR factor RsxA is better translated in the absence of tgt.
source: Proteomics analyses revealed that the anti-SoxR factor RsxA is better translated in the absence of tgt.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing 13-fold higher RsxA levels in Δtgt compared to WT.

claim: RsxA displays a codon bias toward tyrosine TAT.
source: RsxA displays a codon bias toward tyrosine TAT
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis showing 83% TAT codons in rsxA compared to 53% genome average.

claim: Overabundance of RsxA leads to decreased expression of genes belonging to SoxR oxidative stress regulon.
source: overabundance of RsxA leads to decreased expression of genes belonging to SoxR oxidative stress regulon.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing decreased SodA and AcrA levels in Δtgt, and by the known function of RsxA as an anti-SoxR factor.

claim: Regulation of Q34 modification in response to environmental cues leads to translational reprogramming of transcripts bearing a biased tyrosine codon usage.
source: We propose that regulation of Q34 modification in response to environmental cues leads to translational reprogramming of transcripts bearing a biased tyrosine codon usage.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including tgt expression regulation, Q34 level measurements, and differential translation of TAT-biased transcripts.

claim: DNA repair factors are among candidate genes which could be subject to Q34-dependent translational regulation.
source: In silico analysis further identified candidate genes which could be subject to such translational regulation, among which DNA repair factors.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis of codon usage and GO enrichment analysis showing DNA repair genes are TAT-biased.

claim: Many tRNA modification genes are involved in the response to antibiotics from different families.
source: Our recent finding that many tRNA modification genes are involved in the response to antibiotics from different families (Babosan et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The regulatory roles of RNA modifications were first proposed for eukaryotes.
source: The regulatory roles of RNA modifications were first proposed for eukaryotes (Pollo Oliveira and de Crécy Lagard, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The importance of RNA modifications in human diseases has recently emerged.
source: their importance in human diseases has recently emerged (Chujo and Tomizawa, 2021; Suzuki, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Some tRNA modifications are essential in bacteria.
source: In bacteria, while some tRNA modifications are essential (Zhong et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The absence of many RNA modifications shows no growth phenotype in unstressed bacterial cells.
source: the absence of many RNA modification shows no growth phenotype in unstressed cells (de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The roles of tRNA modifications in differential codon decoding have been described in various species.
source: At the molecular level, the roles of tRNA modifications in differential codon decoding have been described in various species (Bruni et al., 1977; Parker, 1982; Taylor et al., 1998; Urbonavicius et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In most cases, no growth phenotype was associated with variations in decoding in bacteria.
source: In most cases, no growth phenotype was associated with these variations in decoding in bacteria.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cited literature on tRNA modifications and codon decoding.

claim: Recent studies highlight the links between tRNA modifications and stress responses in several bacterial species.
source: Recent studies, however, do highlight the links between tRNA modifications and stress responses in several bacterial species (Aubee et al., 2016; Chionh et al., 2016; de Crécy-Lagard and Jaroch, 2021; Fleming et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2017; Thompson and Gottesman, 2014; Thongdee et al., 2019; Večerek et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: New tRNA modifications are still being discovered.
source: and new modifications are still being discovered (Kimura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: TrmD and MiaA have been clearly linked with resistance and persistence to antibiotics via differential codon decoding in cell membrane and efflux proteins.
source: Until recently, few tRNA modification factors have been clearly linked with resistance and persistence to antibiotics, via differential codon decoding in cell membrane and efflux proteins (TrmD [Masuda et al., 2019], MiaA [Taylor et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MoTTs (modification tunable transcripts) are transcripts that will be translated more or less efficiently depending on the presence or absence of tRNA modifications.
source: MoTTs were first (and mostly) defined in eukaryotes as transcripts that will be translated more or less efficiently depending on the presence or absence of tRNA modifications (Endres et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a definition from cited literature.

claim: In E. coli, differential translation of RpoS occurs via MiaA modification affecting leucine codons.
source: differential translation of RpoS/leucine codons via MiaA (Escherichia coli) (Aubee et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, differential translation of Fur occurs via MiaB modification affecting serine codons in response to low iron.
source: Fur/serine codons via MiaB, in response to low iron (E. coli) (Večerek et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Differential translation of MgtA occurs via TrmD modification affecting proline codons in response to low magnesium.
source: MgtA/proline codons via TrmD, in response to low magnesium Hou et al., 2017
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, differential translation of catalases occurs via TrmB modification affecting phenylalanine and aspartate codons during oxidative stress.
source: catalases/phenylalanine and aspartate codons via TrmB, during oxidative stress (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) (Thongdee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mycobacterial response to hypoxic stress features MoTTs.
source: Mycobacterial response to hypoxic stress (Chionh et al., 2016) also features MoTTs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: t/rRNA modifications play a central role in V. cholerae response to stress caused by antibiotics with very different modes of action.
source: During studies in V. cholerae, we recently discovered that t/rRNA modifications play a central role in response to stress caused by antibiotics with very different modes of action (Babosan et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The identified RNA modification genes had not previously been associated with any antibiotic resistance phenotype.
source: The identified RNA modification genes had not previously been associated with any antibiotic resistance phenotype.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of their previous study.

claim: Different tRNA modifications have opposite effects on tolerance to different antibiotics.
source: The fact that different tRNA modifications have opposite effects on tolerance to different antibiotics highlights the complexity of such a network
evidence: This is based on inference from the authors' previous experimental data.

claim: The observed phenotypes are not merely due to a general mistranslation effect.
source: and shows that the observed phenotypes are not merely due to a general mistranslation effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that different modifications have opposite effects.

claim: Deletion of the tgt gene in V. cholerae confers a strong growth defect in the presence of aminoglycosides at doses below the minimal inhibitory concentration.
source: In particular, deletion of the tgt gene encoding tRNA-guanine transglycosylase (Tgt) in V. cholerae confers a strong growth defect in the presence of aminoglycosides at doses below the minimal inhibitory concentration (sub-MIC) (Babosan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Tgt incorporates queuosine (Q) in the place of guanosine (G) in the wobble position of four tRNAs with GUN anticodon.
source: Tgt incorporates queuosine (Q) in the place of guanosine (G) in the wobble position of four tRNAs with GUN anticodon (tRNAAspGUC, tRNAAsnGUU, tRNATyrGUA, tRNAHisGUG) (Ehrenhofer-Murray, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tgt function, supported by citation.

claim: The tRNAs with 'AUN' anticodons are not present in the V. cholerae genome.
source: The tRNAs with 'AUN' anticodons are not present in the genome
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of V. cholerae.

claim: Each one of the four GUN tRNAs decodes two synonymous codons which differ in the third position.
source: and thus each one of the four GUN tRNAs decodes two synonymous codons (aspartate GAC/GAT, asparagine AAC/AAT, tyrosine TAC/TAT, histidine CAC/CAT which differ in the third position).
evidence: This is established knowledge about codon-anticodon pairing and wobble base pairing.

claim: Q34 is known to increase or decrease translation error rates in eukaryotes in a codon and organism-specific manner.
source: Q34 is known to increase or decrease translation error rates in eukaryotes in a codon and organism-specific manner (Ehrenhofer-Murray, 2017; Meier et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Q34 was shown to induce mild oxidative stress resistance in Entamoeba histolytica and to attenuate its virulence.
source: Q34 was shown to induce mild oxidative stress resistance in the eukaryotic parasite Entamoeba histolytica, the causative agent of amebic dysentery, and to attenuate its virulence (Nagaraja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, the absence of Q34 modification was found to decrease mistranslation rates by tRNATyr, while increasing it for tRNAAsp.
source: In E. coli, the absence of Q34 modification was found to decrease mistranslation rates by tRNATyr, while increasing it for tRNAAsp (Manickam et al., 2016; Manickam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No significant biological difference was found in E. coli ∆tgt mutant, except for a slight defect in stationary phase viability.
source: No significant biological difference was found in E. coli ∆tgt mutant, except for a slight defect in stationary phase viability (Noguchi et al., 1982)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: E. coli tgt mutant is involved in biofilm formation.
source: and more recently an involvement in biofilm formation (Díaz Rullo and González Pastor, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The E. coli tgt mutant is more sensitive to aminoglycosides but not to ampicillin nor spectinomycin.
source: Recent studies show that the E. coli tgt mutant is more sensitive to aminoglycosides but not to ampicillin nor spectinomycin
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The E. coli tgt mutant is more sensitive to oxidative stress.
source: and is more sensitive to oxidative stress but the molecular mechanisms were not elucidated (Pollo-Oliveira et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: V. cholerae ∆tgt displays differential decoding of tyrosine TAC vs TAT codons.
source: We find that V. cholerae ∆tgt displays differential decoding of tyrosine TAC vs TAT codons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using GFP reporters with codon stretches.

claim: Several proteins with codon usage biased toward TAT are more efficiently translated in ∆tgt.
source: Molecular reporters, coupled to proteomics and in silico analysis, reveal that several proteins with codon usage biased toward TAT (vs TAC) are more efficiently translated in ∆tgt.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data and ribosome profiling data.

claim: RsxA prevents activation of SoxR oxidative stress response regulon.
source: One of these proteins is RsxA, which prevents activation of SoxR oxidative stress response regulon (Koo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RsxA function, supported by citation.

claim: Tobramycin treatment leads to increased expression of tgt and Q34 modification.
source: We propose that tobramycin treatment leads to increased expression of tgt and Q34 modification
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data showing tgt induction by tobramycin and increased Q34 levels.

claim: Increased tgt expression and Q34 modification allows for more efficient Sox regulon-related oxidative stress response and better response to tobramycin.
source: which in turn allows for more efficient Sox regulon-related oxidative stress response, and better response to tobramycin.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: DNA repair gene transcripts with TAT codon bias are transcripts modulated by Q34 modification.
source: Lastly, bioinformatic analysis identified DNA repair gene transcripts with TAT codon bias as transcripts modulated by Q34 modification
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and UV sensitivity experiments.

claim: V. cholerae ∆tgt shows decreased UV susceptibility.
source: which was confirmed by decreased UV susceptibility of V. cholerae ∆tgt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental UV survival data.

claim: V. cholerae ∆tgt strain has a growth defect in low-dose tobramycin.
source: We confirmed V. cholerae ∆tgt strain's growth defect in low-dose tobramycin (sub-MIC TOB) (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by competition experiment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of tgt in trans restores growth of ∆tgt in sub-MIC tobramycin.
source: and that expression of tgt in trans restores growth in these conditions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by competition experiment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ∆tgt is less tolerant than WT to tobramycin at lethal concentrations.
source: As expected, ∆tgt is less tolerant than WT to tobramycin (Figure 1C and D)
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: ∆tgt has no impact on tolerance to ciprofloxacin or carbenicillin.
source: but had no impact in ciprofloxacin (CIP) or carbenicillin (CRB) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The growth defect of ∆tgt is not due to increased aminoglycoside entry.
source: No changes either in PMF (Figure 1G) or in uptake of the fluorescent aminoglycoside molecule Neomycin-Cy5 (Figure 1H; Sabeti Azad et al., 2020) were detected in the ∆tgt strain, indicating that the increased susceptibility of ∆tgt to TOB is not due to increased aminoglycoside entry into the V. cholerae cell.
evidence: This is supported by PMF and neomycin uptake data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: The growth defect of ∆tgt is not due to a change in proton-motive force.
source: No changes either in PMF (Figure 1G) or in uptake of the fluorescent aminoglycoside molecule Neomycin-Cy5 (Figure 1H; Sabeti Azad et al., 2020) were detected in the ∆tgt strain
evidence: This is supported by PMF measurement data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The absence of Q34 does not affect endogenous tRNA-GUN levels.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of tRNATyr levels showed no major differences between WT and ∆tgt strains, making it unlikely that the effect of Q34 modification on codon decoding is caused by altered synthesis or degradation of tRNATyr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The levels of tRNAHis, tRNAAsn, and tRNAAsp modified by Tgt remain unchanged in ∆tgt.
source: The levels of the other three tRNAs modified by Tgt also remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrGUA rescues the ∆tgt mutant's growth defect in sub-MIC TOB.
source: Overexpression of tRNATyrGUA, but not tRNATyrAUA, rescues the ∆tgt mutant's growth defect in sub-MIC TOB (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by competition experiment data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA does not rescue the ∆tgt mutant's growth defect in sub-MIC TOB.
source: Overexpression of tRNATyrGUA, but not tRNATyrAUA, rescues the ∆tgt mutant's growth defect in sub-MIC TOB (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by competition experiment data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Changes in Tyr codon decoding is mostly responsible for the ∆tgt mutant's tobramycin susceptibility phenotype.
source: We do not observe any major rescue of tobramycin-sensitive phenotypes when the other tRNAs are overexpressed, suggesting that changes in Tyr codon decoding is mostly responsible for the ∆tgt mutant's tobramycin susceptibility phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tRNA overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: GFP fluorescence from native GFP is not affected in ∆tgt compared to WT.
source: First, we confirmed that GFP fluorescence from native GFP (encoded by gfpmut3) is not affected in ∆tgt compared to WT (gfp+ in Figure 2)
evidence: This is supported by GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are no major differences on expression or folding of the GFP in ∆tgt.
source: indicating that there are no major differences on expression or folding of the GFP in ∆tgt.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that native GFP fluorescence is unchanged.

claim: The absence of Q34 leads to an increase of amino acid incorporation at Tyr TAT codons.
source: This set of reporters revealed that the absence of Q34 leads to an increase of amino acid incorporation at Tyr TAT codons, both without and with tobramycin (Figure 2A, NT and TOB).
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of Q34 does not affect amino acid incorporation at Asp codons.
source: This was not the case for Asp (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The absence of Q34 does not affect amino acid incorporation at Asn codons.
source: nor for Asn (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The absence of Q34 has a slight and variable effect on amino acid incorporation at His codons.
source: and we observed a slighter and more variable change for His (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant effect of tgt was observed for second near-cognate codons of TAC and TAT.
source: No significant effect of tgt was observed for second near-cognate codons obtained by changing 1 base of the triplet for TAC and TAT codons (Figure 2E): Phe TTC/TTT, Cys TGT/TGC, Ser TCT/TCC
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Q34 modification strongly impacts the decoding of Tyr codons in the GFP reporter system.
source: Thus, Q34 modification strongly impacts the decoding of Tyr codons, and to a lesser extent His codons in this reporter system.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the GFP reporter data.

claim: Q34 modification impacts the decoding of His codons to a lesser extent than Tyr codons in the GFP reporter system.
source: Thus, Q34 modification strongly impacts the decoding of Tyr codons, and to a lesser extent His codons in this reporter system.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the GFP reporter data.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrGUA facilitates TAC decoding.
source: Overexpression of tRNATyrGUA did not significantly impact decoding of TAT and increased decoding of TAC, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data with tRNA overexpression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Issues with TAC codon decoding contribute to the fitness defect observed in ∆tgt upon growth with tobramycin.
source: Since overexpression of tRNATyrGUA rescues ∆tgt in tobramycin (Figure 1I) and facilitates TAC decoding, this suggests that issues with TAC codon decoding contribute to the fitness defect observed in ∆tgt upon growth with tobramycin.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiment and decoding data.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA increases decoding of TAT in WT.
source: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA increased decoding of TAT in WT but did not change it in ∆tgt where it is already high.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data with tRNA overexpression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA does not change decoding of TAT in ∆tgt.
source: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA increased decoding of TAT in WT but did not change it in ∆tgt where it is already high.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data with tRNA overexpression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA increases decoding of TAC in WT.
source: Unexpectedly, overexpression of tRNATyrAUA also increased decoding of TAC in WT.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data with tRNA overexpression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of tRNATyrAUA may restore translation of TAC-enriched transcripts.
source: Thus, overexpression of tRNATyrAUA possibly changes the equilibrium between the decoding of TAC vs TAT and may restore translation of TAC-enriched transcripts.
evidence: This is speculation based on the unexpected observation of increased TAC decoding.

claim: Tyr103 and Asp129 of β-lactamase are important for its function in resistance to β-lactam antibiotics.
source: The amino acids Tyr103 and Asp129 of the β-lactamase were previously shown to be important for its function in resistance to β-lactam antibiotics, such as carbenicillin (Doucet et al., 2004; Escobar et al., 1994; Jacob et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the WT, both TAC and TAT versions of β-lactamase at position 103 confer similar growth in carbenicillin with or without sub-MIC TOB.
source: While in the WT, both versions of β-lactamase conferred similar growth in carbenicillin with or without sub-MIC TOB
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the ∆tgt strain, the Tyr-TAT version of β-lactamase grows better than the Tyr TAC version upon exposure to TOB stress.
source: in the ∆tgt strain the Tyr-TAT version grows better than the Tyr TAC version upon exposure to TOB stress.
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Tyr103 TAT β-lactamase is translated more efficiently than the native Tyr103 TAC version in stressed ∆tgt strain.
source: This suggests a more efficient translation of the Tyr103 TAT β-lactamase mRNA, compared to the native Tyr103 TAC version, in stressed ∆tgt strain.
evidence: This is an inference from the growth data with β-lactamase reporters.

claim: The GAC version of β-lactamase at position 129 does not produce functional β-lactamase in ∆tgt.
source: When we replaced the native Asp129 GAT with the synonymous codon Asp129 GAC, the GAC version did not appear to produce functional β-lactamase in ∆tgt (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The GAC version of β-lactamase at position 129 suggests increased mistranslation or inefficient decoding of the GAC codon by tRNAAsp in the absence of Q.
source: suggesting increased mistranslation or inefficient decoding of the GAC codon by tRNAAsp in the absence of Q.
evidence: This is an inference from the β-lactamase reporter data.

claim: Decoding of GAT codon is affected in ∆tgt in the presence of tobramycin.
source: Decoding of GAT codon was also affected in ∆tgt in the presence of tobramycin.
evidence: This is supported by β-lactamase reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ∆tgt shows increased readthrough at stop codons UAA and UAG.
source: We found increased readthrough at stop codons UAA and to a lesser extent at UAG for ∆tgt, and this increase was amplified for UAG in presence of tobramycin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, stop readthrough).
evidence: This is supported by stop codon readthrough data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of tobramycin, non-modified tRNATyr mistakenly decodes Asp GAC, His CAC, Ser UCC, Ala GCU, Gly GGU, Leu CUU, and Val GUC codons.
source: Results suggest that in this sequence context, particularly in the presence of tobramycin, non-modified tRNATyr mistakenly decodes Asp GAC, His CAC, and also Ser UCC, Ala GCU, Gly GGU, Leu CUU, and Val GUC codons
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data with near-cognate codons shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Q34 increases the fidelity of tRNATyr.
source: suggesting that Q34 increases the fidelity of tRNATyr.
evidence: This is an inference from the mistranslation data.

claim: Absence of Q34 increases misdecoding by tRNATyr at Asp codons.
source: When the Tyr103 codon was replaced with either Asp codons, we observe increased β-lactamase tolerance (Figure 3D, left), suggesting increased misincorporation of tyrosine by tRNATyr at Asp codons in the absence of Q
evidence: This is supported by β-lactamase tolerance test data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Absence of Q34 decreases misdecoding by tRNAAsp at Tyr UAU.
source: When Asp129 was mutated to Tyr TAT (Figure 3D, right), we observe reduced tolerance in ∆tgt, but not when it was mutated to Tyr TAC, suggesting less misincorporation of aspartate by tRNAAsp at the Tyr UAU codon in the absence of Q.
evidence: This is supported by β-lactamase tolerance test data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Absence of Q34 is involved in translation fidelity during antibiotic stress.
source: This supports the fact that tRNA Q34 modification is involved in translation fidelity during antibiotic stress
evidence: This is a summary inference from the mistranslation and fidelity data.

claim: The effects of Q34 on translation fidelity can be different on different tRNAs.
source: and that the effects can be different on different tRNAs, e.g., tRNATyr and tRNAAsp tested here.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of opposite effects on tRNATyr and tRNAAsp.

claim: Loss of Q34 results in generally decreased detection of many proteins in tobramycin.
source: Loss of Q34 results in generally decreased detection of many proteins in tobramycin (shift toward the left in the volcano plot; Figure 4AB)
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4AB.

claim: Loss of Q34 results in increases in the levels of 96 proteins.
source: and in increases in the levels of 96 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: RsxA is 13-fold more abundant in the ∆tgt strain compared to WT in tobramycin.
source: Among those, RsxA (encoded by VC1017) is 13-fold more abundant in the ∆tgt strain compared to WT in tobramycin.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: SoxR controls sodA and acrA among other genes of the regulon.
source: SoxR is an oxidative stress response regulator (Koo et al., 2003) that controls sodA (VC2694, superoxide dismutase) and acrA (VC0913, efflux), among other genes of the regulon.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The levels of SodA and AcrA proteins are decreased in ∆tgt compared to WT in TOB.
source: Consistently, we find that the levels of SodA and AcrA proteins are decreased in ∆tgt compared to WT in TOB (indicated in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RsxA has 83% of Tyr TAT codons instead of the expected 53% average.
source: With 83% of Tyr TAT codons, instead of the expected 53% average, RsxA has a clear codon usage bias.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis of codon usage.

claim: No statistically significant difference in TAT codon usage was detected in the sets of more abundant or less abundant proteins in ∆tgt TOB.
source: No statistically significant difference was detected for TAT codon usage in neither sets of proteins.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of codon usage in proteomics data.

claim: One cannot draw conclusions about codon decoding efficiencies in ∆tgt from the proteomics data alone.
source: Thus, one cannot draw conclusions or infer predictions about codon decoding efficiencies in a tRNA modification mutant such as ∆tgt from the proteomics data alone.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of clear codon usage patterns in proteomics data.

claim: Ribo-seq analysis determined 159 transcripts with increased translation in ∆tgt.
source: However, we determined 159 transcripts with increased and 197 with decreased translation in ∆tgt
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data.

claim: Ribo-seq analysis determined 197 transcripts with decreased translation in ∆tgt.
source: However, we determined 159 transcripts with increased and 197 with decreased translation in ∆tgt
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data.

claim: TAT codon usage was decreased in the list of transcripts with decreased translation efficiency in ∆tgt.
source: Ribo-seq data (Supplementary file 2) shows that TAT codon usage was decreased in the list of transcripts with decreased translation efficiency in ∆tgt
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: TAT codon usage was increased in the list of transcripts with increased translation efficiency in ∆tgt.
source: while it was increased in the list of transcripts with increased translation efficiency (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: No difference in AAT and CAT codon usage was detected in transcripts with differential translation efficiency in ∆tgt.
source: No difference was detected for AAT and CAT (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis showed 53 genes significantly downregulated in ∆tgt in MH.
source: Transcriptomic analysis comparing at least twofold differentially expressed genes between V. cholerae ∆tgt and WT strains (Supplementary file 3) showed that, respectively, 53 and 26 genes were significantly downregulated in MH and tobramycin
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis showed 26 genes significantly downregulated in ∆tgt in tobramycin.
source: Transcriptomic analysis comparing at least twofold differentially expressed genes between V. cholerae ∆tgt and WT strains (Supplementary file 3) showed that, respectively, 53 and 26 genes were significantly downregulated in MH and tobramycin
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis showed 34 genes significantly upregulated in ∆tgt in tobramycin.
source: and 34 were up in tobramycin.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The most impacted GO categories in MH were bacteriocin transport and iron import into the cell.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that the most impacted GO categories were bacteriocin transport and iron import into the cell (45- and 40-fold enriched) in MH
